title: UMAP's Forgotten Graph: Network Science for Free Sensemaking
hook: Everyone uses UMAP for its 2D scatter plot and throws away the graph it builds along the way — a graph that's still faithful to the data manifold, and worth analyzing on its own.
key_points: UMAP builds a k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) graph in the original high-dimensional space before projecting to 2D; typical workflows discard this graph and keep only the projection.
PageRank on this graph identifies representative data points, without any purpose-built exemplar-selection method.
k-core decomposition reveals dense core regions versus sparse periphery in the data.
Clustering coefficient detects tight-knit neighborhoods of highly similar points.

On MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, these off-the-shelf graph algorithms are competitive with or complementary to purpose-built methods like k-medoids (exemplar selection) and HDBSCAN (density-based clustering).
content_html: UMAP is one of the most-used tools for visualizing high-dimensional data, but almost everyone only looks at its output: the 2D scatter plot. Along the way, UMAP builds something else — a k-nearest-neighbor graph in the original high-dimensional space — and that graph gets thrown away once the plot is made.
extra_html:
Researchers from Georgia Tech and Apple argue that graph shouldn't be wasted. Because it's constructed before the distortion that any 2D projection introduces, it's a more faithful encoding of the data manifold than the picture people actually look at. The paper shows three standard network-science algorithms applied directly to this graph do useful sensemaking work: PageRank surfaces representative data points, k-core decomposition separates dense core regions from a sparser periphery, and clustering coefficient flags tight-knit neighborhoods of highly similar points.

Tested quantitatively and qualitatively on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, these general-purpose graph analyses turn out to be competitive with, or complementary to, methods purpose-built for the same jobs — k-medoids for picking exemplars, HDBSCAN for density-based clustering. The takeaway for practitioners: if you're already running UMAP, its internal graph is a second, underused source of insight into your data, not just plumbing on the way to a plot.

related.title: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
related.hook: Find the directions your data varies most, then keep only the top few - you compress many correlated features into a handful while retaining most of the signal.

related.title: k-Means Clustering
related.hook: Pick k cluster centers, assign every point to the nearest one, move each center to the mean of its points, repeat - clusters emerge without any labels.

flashcards.prompt: What part of UMAP's own pipeline does this paper argue gets thrown away, and why does that matter?
flashcards.back_html: UMAP internally builds a kNN graph over the data in its original high-dimensional space before projecting to 2D. That graph is discarded once the 2D embedding is made, even though it's undistorted by the 2D projection and encodes the data manifold directly.

flashcards.prompt: What does applying k-core decomposition to UMAP's internal kNN graph reveal?

choices.text: Dense core regions of the data versus its sparse periphery
The optimal number of 2D dimensions to project onto
Which two data points are most dissimilar

flashcards.explanation_html: k-core decomposition is a network-science technique that separates a graph into progressively denser cores; applied here it surfaces which parts of the data are densely interconnected versus peripheral.

flashcards.prompt: How did the graph-based analyses (PageRank, k-core, clustering coefficient) compare to purpose-built methods like k-medoids and HDBSCAN on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST?
flashcards.back_html: Competitive with or complementary to them — general network-science tools applied to a graph UMAP builds for free rivaled methods designed specifically for exemplar selection and density-based clustering.
